Studies on the chemistry of rock glaciers and mountain permafrost (sulfate, Ni, Zn, Al, Fe) are kept even when acidity is low, because they document the same process (sulfide oxidation triggered by thaw). Purely hydrological studies (without chemistry) were excluded.

Grey literature (theses, INAIGEM/USGS/CGS reports, GSA/EGU abstracts, a TCD discussion paper, a popular-science article in The Conversation) is kept but flagged peer_reviewed=false.

refs.title: Acidic Mine Drainage: The Rate-Determining Step
refs.publisher: American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)
refs.question: What is the rate-limiting step in pyrite oxidation and acid production in waters draining coal and copper mines?
refs.methods: Kinetic aqueous-chemistry approach (the abstract does not detail the protocol).
refs.results: Oxidation of ferrous iron to ferric iron is identified as the rate-limiting step of pyrite oxidation and acidification; controlling this reaction is necessary to combat the pollution.
refs.contribution: Foundational reference on the ARD mechanism: central role of the Fe2+/Fe3+ couple, basis for later work on microbial catalysis.

refs.title: Aqueous pyrite oxidation by dissolved oxygen and by ferric iron
refs.question: What are the rates and pathways of abiotic pyrite oxidation in solution, by dissolved oxygen on the one hand and by ferric iron on the other?
refs.methods: Laboratory experiments without microorganisms, in O2-saturated solutions or in anoxic Fe(III)-saturated solutions, at initial pH from 2 to 9; monitoring of intermediate sulfur species.
refs.results: In the presence of O2, the oxidation rate varies little with pH; thiosulfate and polythionates appear above pH 3.9 (and only under strong stirring). Oxidation by Fe(III) is faster, with no intermediates detected (except traces of sulfite at pH 9).
refs.contribution: Foundational reference: the authors conclude that Fe(III) is the direct oxidant of pyrite in both systems, making this a basic paper for ARD mechanisms.

refs.site: upper Alamosa River basin (Stunner, Summitville/Cropsy Creek, Cat Creek, Jasper, Crater Creek), San Juan, Colorado

refs.question: Establish the natural geochemical background of waters draining unmined pyritic altered zones around the Summitville mine, in order to inform remediation goals.

refs.title: Schwertmannite and the chemical modeling of iron in acid sulfate waters
refs.site: 28 mine drainage sites; one naturally acidic alpine stream
refs.question: Which iron oxyhydroxides and oxyhydroxysulfates precipitate as a function of pH in acid sulfate waters, and how can schwertmannite be integrated into chemical modelling of iron?
refs.methods: Analysis of ochre precipitates and associated waters at 28 mine drainage sites, calculation of ion activity products, long-term equilibration experiment, pe-pH diagram of the Fe-S-K-O-H system and a non-equilibrium reaction-path model applied to a naturally acidic alpine stream.
refs.results: Ferrihydrite (± goethite) above pH 6.5; schwertmannite dominant between pH 2.8 and 4.5; jarosite notable in a single sample (pH 2.6). Schwertmannite log IAP = 18.0 ± 2.5; goethite log K = 1.40 ± 0.01; a synthetic schwertmannite fully transformed to goethite in 543 days.
refs.contribution: Establishes the paragenetic sequence jarosite – schwertmannite – ferrihydrite – goethite and a metastability field for schwertmannite, a basic tool for interpreting ferruginous precipitates of both mining and natural ARD.

refs.title: Acid rock drainage and climate change
refs.site: three mine sites in the United States and other sites worldwide
refs.question: How do climate variability (droughts, storms) and climate change modulate acidity and metal concentrations in waters draining mine wastes and mineralized areas?

refs.results: Concentrations increase slowly during dry periods and then rise sharply at the onset of the first storm's flood (“first flush”), before falling below the initial level at peak discharge; this is due to dissolution of soluble salts and flushing of evapoconcentrated waters. refs.site: 95 glacierized basins (global compilation)
refs.question: Does glacial weathering differ chemically from non-glacial weathering, and does enhanced sulfide oxidation make glacierized basins a CO2 source?
refs.methods: Compilation of 7700 samples from 95 glacierized basins compared with large rivers and the GloRiCh database; Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests on elemental ratios; Monte-Carlo mixing model to partition solutes among silicates, carbonates, evaporites and atmospheric inputs; order-of-magnitude CO2 calculations.
refs.results: Median SO4:Na ratio of about 1.0 in glacial basins versus 0.4 for non-glacial rivers (sulfide oxidation about 2.5 times stronger); median Ca:Na of about 4.3 versus 0.7 to 1.1. About 20 % of glacial basins indicate net CO2 release; glacial oxidation could change ocean-atmosphere CO2 by about 25 ppm over 10,000 years under Last Glacial Maximum-like conditions.
refs.contribution: Establishes at the global scale that glacial waters are marked by sulfide oxidation, providing a global framework for natural ARD in glacial settings.

refs.question: Does permafrost thaw cause abrupt acidification of headwater streams through accelerated sulfide oxidation, and is this signal visible in large rivers downstream?
refs.methods: Time series of pH, sulfate, metals and conductivity as a function of discharge, sampling of acidic seeps and vegetation dieback zones, remote sensing, mineralogy of precipitates, S and O isotopes of sulfate, fluxes and CO₂ from C-Q relationships, long-term trends in riverine sulfate.
refs.results: Dozens of acidic seeps appeared within ten years (median pH 3.1; sulfate up to 17,610 mg/L; Al up to 1,277 mg/L). At KM175, pH fell from 7.5 (2019-2022) to 2.7 in 2025; at KM228, pH 3.3 and 10,800 mg/L sulfate were measured (July 2025). Satellite imagery identifies 146 affected reaches in the Peel basin. Peel sulfate increases by 2.1 mg/L/yr (2000-2025), but metals remain stable downstream owing to attenuation.
refs.contribution: Major regional-scale demonstration of abrupt natural ARD caused by permafrost degradation, with effects on metals, sulfur and carbon (CO₂ emissions).

refs.note: Author version read on the HARVEST repository (USask); supplementary material not read.

refs.title: Rapidly thawing permafrost is acidifying streams across North America
refs.site: central Yukon (Tombstone Waters Observatory, Tombstone Territorial Park, Engineer Creek)
refs.question: Is rapid permafrost thaw acidifying streams in north-western North America?
refs.methods: Popular-science article presenting a water-monitoring study conducted in central Yukon with the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in First Nation.
refs.results: Streams are acidifying abruptly, sometimes within a few years, and turning orange or milky white over several kilometres: thaw allows water to react with sulfides and release acid, sulfate, iron, aluminium and toxic metals. Large rivers appear for now to be buffered by neutralisation and dilution. No figures are given.
refs.contribution: Reports a natural ARD phenomenon triggered by permafrost thaw at a large scale; to be complemented by the cited scientific article (DOI 10.1126/science.aea2898).
refs.found_via: cites seed Zarroca2021, Garcia2025; Crossref keywords “thawing permafrost metals stream”
refs.note: Popular-science article in The Conversation (republished by McMaster University), not peer-reviewed; read in full. The underlying scientific article (probably Science, DOI 10.1126/science.aea2898) was not read.

refs.title: Permafrost‐Thaw Driven Acid‐Rock Drainage Threatens Arctic Aquatic Ecosystems
refs.site: permafrost zone of north-western North America (Brooks Range, Alaska; Yukon)
refs.question: What is the regional extent of permafrost-thaw-related ARD in north-western North America, in light of recent studies (Evinger et al. 2026; Skierszkan et al. 2026a)?
refs.methods: Opinion article (Viewpoint) placing recent studies in their regional context.
refs.contribution: Presents thaw-related ARD as one of the most important recently recognised environmental hazards: abrupt onset in the Brooks Range and release of acidity and metals at toxic concentrations from thousands of seeps across the permafrost zone.
